What did it mean that they had public voice, as well as an income? Were they still women? Or were they now something else, something infinitely more threatening than the ever-tractable and ever-contained Angel in the House?
It was, to say the least, a confusing time to be a woman, and an even more confusing time to think about women, or to try to get a handle on them culturally.

It’s no wonder, then, that Hollywood produced a whole genre of horror films about women who were both human and inhuman, both passive and predatory, full of self-hatred yet also full of hatred for men. Sometimes these inhuman women were innocent victims, caught in the throes of an evil man’s corrupt schemes; sometimes these inhuman women were tethered to some horrific, ancient, supernatural evil that lurked in their blood.

As a result of these changes, the Monstrous Bitch of the twentieth century is much less about reproductive horror or violence against children and much more about sexual violence, sexual deviance, and the idea that there’s something ancient and animalistic in women that modern medicine and psychoanalysis will never quite be able to control, no matter how hard they try.

Our first hypersexual female monster of the silver screen appears in Dracula’s Daughter: Marya Zaleska, the daughter of the recently slain Dracula. As an outright vampire, she is a collection of paradoxes: She’s human but also a monster; she’s not alive, nor is she dead; she’s bloodthirsty and predatory, but she’s also charming and outrageously sexy.

By contrast, Marya wants to cure herself of the supernatural monstrosity she holds within her. She wants to get “well”; she understands her vampirism, then, as a disease, something she can perhaps treat with science and medicine. So she seeks help from a psychoanalyst named Dr. Jeffrey Garth, who, conveniently, is also a terrible rake, snob, and low-grade abuser of women.

But then, we shouldn’t be surprised, nor disappointed. Of course the treatment fails: Marya’s not mentally ill; she’s a vampire. Part of what this film seems to be saying to the fantasy of Freudian efficacy at explaining female monstrosity by recourse to psychosexual dynamics is that there’s something in the Monstrous Bitch that exceeds the capacity of medicine to treat or the talking cure to talk away.

As in Lilith. As in Lilitu. The ancient Monstrous Bitch from Mesopotamia is reaching her bloody claw forward to the twentieth century and the era of science and psychoanalysis to say, Nope, you’re not taking this one from me.

There is something old in Irena that she simply cannot escape. The films, while seeming to endorse the psychoanalytic method of wrangling female monstrosity, actually poke holes in that method, showing it to be utterly inadequate to the task at hand.

He made her literally by splicing two different women’s body parts—glands and brain—into the body of a gorilla. He is thus both a torturer of animals and a femicide, and Paula is born from his violence, his ambition, and his desire to control nature. She is born of patriarchal science run riot.

This sea creature is a ringer for Tiamat, the Mesopotamian goddess of the sea: Like Tiamat, this sea creature is reptilian, like a basilisk or dragon. Like Tiamat, she’s also marked by hypersexuality and hyperfemaleness. She has huge breasts and long hair.

A woman who was greedy and ambitious, like Marilyn. A woman who would stop at nothing to have her way, seducing and betraying men indiscriminately along the way, in pursuit of power and wealth on her own terms. Marilyn is a sexy, ambitious, modern-day, and decisively capitalistic Tiamat or Lilitu.

Wasp Woman shares with her foremothers the bloodsucking, the sexual rapacity, the shrill and emasculating mouth, and the animality. Like her more recent sisters-in-bloodlust, she has a backstory that is dually psychoanalytic and scientific, though in this case much less empathogenic than Andrea’s, Paula’s, Irena’s, or even Marya’s. The only monstrous woman who’s even close to as bad as the Wasp Woman is Marilyn from Voodoo Woman.

These films, then, appear to see exactly what I’ve been arguing about the nature of the Monstrous Bitch throughout this book, which is that Monstrous Bitches are not a “natural” cultural phenomenon but are created by patriarchal control. Put otherwise, Monstrous Bitchery is caused by patriarchal interference with women—even if it is also against Patriarchy that the Monstrous Bitch rails, bites, and claws.

And in all cases, the fundamental mechanism that these films use to understand how the past keeps revisiting itself on the present is the mechanism of possession. The past Monstrous Bitch surges up to take possession of the young women of today. And that past Monstrous Bitch is loudmouthed, hypersexual, and once again eager to commit violence on young people in particular, be they babies or young girls.
